questions.q: What makes an operation idempotent?
options: It always returns byte-identical response bodies to every caller who repeats it
Repeating it leaves the system in the same state as running it once
It performs no writes or side effects of any kind
It executes atomically inside a single transaction

questions.q: Which HTTP method is NOT defined as idempotent by the spec?
options: PUT
DELETE
GET
POST

questions.q: How does a server typically use an idempotency key?
options: It stores the key with the first result and replays that result on retries
It hashes the key into a response signature that clients verify on every retry
It derives the database shard for the write from the key
It rate-limits each client according to its key

questions.q: A request times out. Why is blindly retrying a non-idempotent operation risky?
options: Timeouts prove the server never received the request
Retries are only permitted on GET by HTTP rules
The first attempt may have succeeded, so the retry can duplicate it
The network guarantees at-most-once delivery, so retries get rejected upstream

questions.q: A client DELETEs a resource twice; the second call returns 404. Is DELETE still idempotent?
options: No — the differing status codes break idempotency
No — unless the server returns 200 for both calls
Only if the server implements soft deletes so the row still exists afterward
Yes — idempotency concerns the resulting state, not identical responses

questions.q: How is 'exactly-once' processing actually achieved in practice?
options: TCP already guarantees exactly-once delivery end to end
At-least-once delivery combined with idempotent, deduplicating processing
Brokers like Kafka fully remove any need for consumer-side deduplication logic
Two-phase commit spanning every service in the request path

questions.q: Which operation is naturally idempotent without extra machinery?
options: Increment the login counter by one
Append a new row to the audit log recording the attempt
Set the user's shipping address to a given value
Charge the customer's card ten dollars

questions.q: Why can PUT create resources idempotently while POST typically cannot?
options: PUT targets a client-chosen URI, so repeats address the same resource
PUT requests are transparently deduplicated by proxies along the path
POST bodies are forbidden from carrying identifiers
PUT skips the server-side validation that POST must run

questions.q: A retry with the same idempotency key arrives while the original request is still executing. Best server behavior?
options: Process the retry as an independent new operation
Return 200 immediately with an empty body
Recognize the in-flight key; wait or return a conflict, then serve the original's result
Evict the key and restart the operation from scratch

questions.q: Idempotency keys expire after 1 minute, but clients retry for up to 10 minutes. What can happen?
options: A late retry lands after expiry and the operation executes twice
Retries fail with 409 until the client generates a fresh key
Key collisions between unrelated clients silently corrupt each other's stored responses
The dedupe table grows without bound and exhausts storage

questions.q: A client reuses an idempotency key with a different request body. Best server behavior?
options: Execute the new body and overwrite the stored result
Merge the two payloads and process the union
Silently return the original stored response and discard the new body without any signal
Reject with an error indicating the key was reused with a mismatched payload

questions.q: A queue redelivers messages occasionally, and the consumer inserts an order per message. How do you prevent duplicate orders?
options: Enable the broker's exactly-once flag and remove all consumer-side checks
Record processed message IDs in the same transaction as the insert
Slow the consumer down until redelivery stops occurring
Hash the order contents client-side before sending

questions.q: A POST /charge with no idempotency support times out. Safest client policy?
options: Query the charge's status server-side before attempting any retry
Retry immediately up to three times, then alert
Retry with exponential backoff, which makes duplication impossible
Reissue the request as a PUT so it becomes idempotent

questions.q: What is the simplest robust backstop against duplicate order rows from retries?
options: An application-level check-then-insert before every write
Comparing recent orders by amount and timestamp heuristically before inserting
A read-through cache in front of the orders table
A unique constraint on a client-supplied operation ID

questions.q: The server completes a payment but crashes before saving the idempotency record. A retry arrives. Result?
options: The retry safely returns the cached response from the log
The payment may execute twice — the record and the write were not atomic
The stale key blocks the retry until an operator clears it
The database automatically detects the orphaned write and rolls the payment back

questions.q: A proxy retries failed requests against another backend. Why is this dangerous for POSTs?
options: Request bodies are silently stripped whenever proxies replay them to a second backend
Proxies cannot re-establish TLS for a replayed request
The first attempt may have executed, so the replay duplicates the side effect
It defeats sticky sessions and misroutes the user

questions.q: Service A dedupes with idempotency keys, then calls B without one. A times out on B and retries. What can happen?
options: Nothing — A's dedupe layer covers the whole call chain
B rejects the retry because TCP sequence numbers repeat across connections
A's key store detects the downstream duplicate and compensates
B's side effect duplicates — dedupe must extend end to end

questions.q: Idempotency keys live in a cache with LRU eviction. What failure emerges under memory pressure?
options: Evicted keys let retried operations execute a second time
Cache misses add latency to every write path
Keys leak across tenant boundaries when evicted slabs are reused by other accounts
TTLs silently reset each time a key is read

questions.q: Two identical requests with one key arrive simultaneously; both find no stored record and both execute. Fix?
options: Extend the key TTL so later duplicates are caught
Atomically claim the key with a unique insert before executing; the loser waits or errors
Shard the key store aggressively so lookups always finish before execution begins
Compare payload hashes after both executions complete

questions.q: A consumer dedupes by message ID in its database, then sends an email. Duplicate emails still occur. Why?
options: Message IDs are not unique across queue partitions
SMTP relays retry deliveries internally no matter what the sending application does
The send is not atomic with the dedupe commit — a crash between them causes resend
The dedupe table's TTL expires before redelivery stops
